The Inverse z-Transform and LTI System Analysis (L08)

Why this matters in the exam: L08 has never been tested (Sample Test 1 covers only L02–L04), so it is fresh material for the final. It is also the engine behind later topics: T6 Q2 (convolution by z-transform), T8 Q5(c) (stable inverse of a channel) and all of T7 end with “now invert using the ROC”. Expect at least one multi-part calculation question worth roughly 5–10 marks: partial fractions → pick the right sequence from the ROC → say if the system is causal/stable → possibly the difference equation. Every step is mechanical once you have the playbook, so these are marks you can bank.

1. The core ideas

1.1 Partial fractions in form (L08 slide 4)

1.2 The ROC of the total is the intersection (L08 slide 4)

The overall ROC is the intersection of the term ROCs. So, for a given overall ROC:

  • every pole inside the inner edge of the ROC (ROC lies outside it) gives a causal term;
  • every pole outside the outer edge (ROC lies inside it) gives an anti-causal term.

With poles at distinct radii there are possible ROCs (rings bounded by poles, L07 slide 17), so possible signals. The other sign combinations give an empty ROC and are not valid (T7 Q1 solution lists one with “ROC: ∅”).

1.3 Numerator degree denominator degree: long division first

Partial fractions only work for a proper fraction in : numerator degree < denominator degree (degrees counted in powers of ). If , divide first:

  • shortcut: the quotient is a constant (ratio of the highest powers of ). T8 Q5(c): gives .

1.5 Power series (L08 slide 5)

The coefficient of is . So the coefficient of is . For a polynomial (finite sequence) just read it off. For a rational , long division gives the terms one at a time:

  • causal ROC: divide in ascending powers of (constant terms first) → series in ;

Long division gives numbers, not a closed form. Use it to get the first few samples, or to check a partial-fraction answer.

1.6 Transfer function, LCCDE, causality and stability (L08 slides 7–11)

Property Test on (rational)
Causal ROC is the exterior of a circle, including
Anti-causal ROC is the interior of a circle, with a zero at the origin
Stable (BIBO) ROC includes the unit circle
Causal and stable all poles strictly inside the unit circle
Anti-causal and stable all poles outside the unit circle
System Poles and zeros Other names
FIR finite zeros, th-order pole at all-zero, moving average (MA). Always stable
All-pole finite poles, th-order zero at autoregressive (AR)
General IIR ratio of both poles and zeros pole-zero (ARMA)
  • Trap: sign of the . With terms all on the left, , the denominator is , same signs. If the question writes , move it across first: denominator .
  • Trap: “stable” is about the ROC, not about the poles alone. Poles at and can be stable (ring ROC) or unstable (outer ROC).

2. The method

Recognise the question.

Wording Playbook
“Determine ” + an ROC A
“All possible signals” / no ROC given B
“If is absolutely summable” / “stable” / “has a DTFT” B, then pick the ring containing
“First few samples” / polynomial in C
“Produces output for input ” D
“Difference equation” ↔︎ “” E
“Is it causal / stable?” F

A. Inverse by partial fractions (one ROC given)

  1. Write in powers of . Make each denominator factor monic: . Pull constants out to the front.
  2. Compare degrees in . If numerator degree denominator degree, long-divide (or use the shortcut ) to get the polynomial part plus a proper remainder.
  3. Find each by cover-up at . Check: at the expansion must equal .
  4. Mark each pole against the ROC. ROC outside the pole → causal . ROC inside the pole → anti-causal .
  5. Add the terms. Write the ROC next to the answer.

B. All possible signals / the stable one

  1. Do A steps 1–3 once. The algebra is the same for every ROC.
  2. Sort the pole radii. List the ROCs: , , …, .
  3. For each ROC apply A step 4. Present it as a table or a braced list (the T7 Q1 solution layout).
  4. Label each: causal (outer ROC), anti-causal (inner ROC, if there is a zero at the origin), two-sided (ring).
  5. “Absolutely summable” = stable = has a DTFT = ROC contains . At most one ROC qualifies. If a pole sits on , none does.

C. Power series / long division

  1. Polynomial in and : coefficient of is . Mark the sample with ↑.
  2. Rational, causal: write numerator and denominator in ascending powers of . Divide. Each quotient term gives .
  3. Rational, left-sided: write both in descending powers of (i.e. ascending powers of ). Divide. Quotient term gives .

  1. Find and with their ROCs (use shift: ).
  2. Combine each into a single fraction. Factor.
  3. . Cancel common factors. Expand the denominator if the LCCDE is wanted.
  4. ROC of : use the given property (e.g. “causal” → outside the largest pole of ). It must be consistent with .

E. ↔︎ LCCDE

  1. LCCDE: write . Replace and .
  2. LCCDE : z-transform both sides term by term, collect and , divide.
  3. The LCCDE does not fix the ROC. You need “causal” or “stable” as extra information.

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Dropping the minus sign on anti-causal terms. with is . Writing instead of is also wrong.
  • Non-monic factors. T7 Q1’s must become before cover-up, or every coefficient is off by a factor of 3.
  • Doing partial fractions on an improper fraction. If numerator degree denominator degree in , you lose the terms. Quick test: always gives a constant .
  • Using the wrong ratio for the constant. It is the ratio of the highest-power coefficients (0.64/(−1.2) in T8 Q5), not of the constant terms.
  • Choosing terms by “pole inside unit circle → causal”. Causal or anti-causal comes from each pole’s position relative to the ROC, not the unit circle. The unit circle only decides which ROC is the stable one.
  • Listing “possible signals”. Only ROCs exist. Combinations with an empty ROC are not valid signals; say so if you write them down.
  • Sign errors moving between and the LCCDE. gives denominator , not .
  • Leaving complex exponentials in the answer for a complex pole pair. Combine to .

7. Add to your open-book reference sheet

INVERSE z (L08)  -- work in w = z^-1, factors as (1 - p w)
A_i = [(1 - p_i w) X]_{w = 1/p_i}      check: sum A_i (+quotient) = X at w=0
A/(1-p z^-1):  |z|>|p| -> A p^n u(n)        |z|<|p| -> -A p^n u(-n-1)
Double pole: 1/(1-pz^-1)^2 -> (n+1)p^n u(n)  |  -(n+1)p^n u(-n-1)
             find A2 by cover-up, then A1 from w = 0
Complex pair p = r e^{j th}:  2|A| r^n cos(th n + angle A) u(n)
                            = 2 r^n [ReA cos th n - ImA sin th n] u(n)
Improper (M >= N in z^-1): divide first; M = N -> constant b_N/a_N
   (ratio of HIGHEST z^-1 coeffs) -> constant*delta(n)
ROC: poles inside ROC's inner edge -> causal terms; outside outer edge -> anti-causal
N distinct pole radii -> N+1 ROCs -> N+1 signals. Stable = ROC contains |z|=1
Power series: coeff of z^-n = x(n). Causal: divide ascending z^-1.
   Left-sided: divide ascending z (highest z^-1 power first)
System ID: H = Y/X (factor, cancel); ROC from "causal"/"stable"; R_y >= R_h n R_x
LCCDE <-> H: y(n) + sum a_k y(n-k) = sum b_k x(n-k)  <->  H = B(z^-1)/(1 + sum a_k z^-k)
   LCCDE alone does not fix the ROC
Causal <-> ROC outside outermost pole (incl. inf). Stable <-> ROC has |z|=1.
Causal+stable <-> all poles |p|<1. Anti-causal+stable <-> all |p|>1.
FIR (MA): M zeros, Mth-order pole at 0, always stable.
All-pole (AR): N poles, Nth-order zero at 0.
